{{Short description|Low-rank isomorphisms in mathematics}}

In [[mathematics]], the '''exceptional isomorphisms of classical groups''' (also: '''accidental isomorphism''' or '''sporadic isogenies''') are unexpected coincidences between different families of [[symmetry group]]s in small dimensions. They occur because some constructions that are different in general become equivalent at low rank. A trivial example is the familiar fact that the [[unit complex number]]s form a group under complex multiplication, denoted <math>\mathrm U(1)</math>, that is the same as the group <math>\mathrm{SO}(2)</math> of [[rotation group|rotations]] of the [[Euclidean plane]]. A less trivial example is the [[covering group|double covering]] <math>\mathrm{SU}(2)\to\mathrm{SO}(3)</math>, which relates [[special unitary matrix|special unitary 2×2 matrices]] to [[3D rotation group|rotations of 3-dimensional Euclidean space]], and provides the simplest example of the connection between rotation groups and [[spinor]]s.

More precisely, these are [[rank of a Lie algebra|low-rank]] [[isomorphism]]s or [[isogeny|central isogenies]] among [[classical group|classical algebraic groups]] that arise from accidental identifications of the corresponding [[root system]]s, specifically <math>A_1=B_1=C_1</math>, <math>D_2 = A_1\times A_1</math>, <math>B_2=C_2</math>, and <math>A_3=D_3</math>. These isomorphisms may be realized concretely through small [[linear representation]]s, and over the [[real numbers]] they give rise to corresponding isomorphisms for several noncompact [[real form]]s. Some, such as <math>\mathrm{Spin}^+(1,3)\cong\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbf C)</math> and <math>\mathrm{Spin}^+(2,4)\cong\mathrm{SU}(2,2)</math>, have applications in [[general relativity]], [[string theory]], and other areas of [[mathematical physics]].

Over more general fields, these exceptional isomorphisms persist for non-split forms and are described uniformly using [[central simple algebra]]s with involution, [[Clifford algebra]]s, and related constructions. In this form they identify not only split orthogonal, symplectic, and unitary groups, but also their [[Inner form|inner and outer forms]]. These exceptional isomorphisms are important in the structure theory of [[algebraic group]]s and in the study of [[automorphic form]]s, [[theta correspondence]], and the [[Langlands program]].

== Over algebraically closed fields ==

Over an [[algebraically closed field]] of [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] not 2, the exceptional isomorphisms of classical groups arise from accidental identifications among the low-rank [[Dynkin diagram]]s and the corresponding [[root system]]s.<ref name="ConradRootCalc">{{cite web
 |last=Conrad
 |first=Brian
 |title=Math 210C. Calculation of some root systems
 |url=https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/210CPage/handouts/rootcalc.pdf
 |website=Stanford University
}}</ref><ref name="KMRT">{{cite book
 |last1=Knus
 |first1=Max-Albert |author-link=Max-Albert Knus
 |last2=Merkurjev
 |first2=Alexander |author-link2=Alexander Merkurjev
 |last3=Rost
 |first3=Markus |author-link3=Markus Rost
 |last4=Tignol
 |first4=Jean-Pierre |author-link4=Jean-Pierre Tignol
 |title=The Book of Involutions
 |series=American Mathematical Society Colloquium Publications
 |volume=44
 |publisher=American Mathematical Society
 |location=Providence, RI
 |year=1998
 |isbn=978-0-8218-0904-4
}}</ref> At the level of [[simple Lie algebra]]s these are
<math display="block">
A_1=B_1=C_1,\qquad
A_1\times A_1=D_2,\qquad
B_2=C_2,\qquad
A_3=D_3.
</math>
Passing from Lie algebras to simply connected algebraic groups gives the corresponding low-rank isomorphisms among the classical groups.<ref name="ConradOq">{{cite web
 |last=Conrad
 |first=Brian
 |title=Algebraic Groups I: Properties of Orthogonal Groups
 |url=https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/252Page/handouts/O%28q%29.pdf
 |website=Stanford University
}}</ref><ref name="KMRT" />

In low dimensions these isomorphisms also admit concrete topological realizations. The circle group may be identified with the rotation group of the Euclidean plane,
<math display="block">
\mathrm U(1)\cong \mathrm{SO}(2),
</math>
and the group of unit quaternions gives the compact form
<math display="block">
\mathrm{SU}(2)\cong \mathrm{Spin}(3)\cong \mathrm{Sp}(1).
</math>
Continuing in this way gives
<math display="block">
\mathrm{Spin}(4)\cong \mathrm{SU}(2)\times \mathrm{SU}(2),\qquad
\mathrm{Spin}(5)\cong \mathrm{Sp}(2),\qquad
\mathrm{Spin}(6)\cong \mathrm{SU}(4).
</math>
These are the compact real forms of the complex isomorphisms listed above.<ref name="ConradLie">{{cite web
 |last1=Conrad
 |first1=Brian
 |last2=Landesman
 |first2=Aaron
 |title=Math 210C. Compact Lie groups
 |url=https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/210CPage/handouts/lie_groups_notes.pdf
 |website=Stanford University
}}</ref><ref name="Vistoli">{{cite web
 |last=Vistoli
 |first=Angelo |author-link=Angelo Vistoli
 |title=Notes on Clifford algebras, spin groups and triality
 |url=https://homepage.sns.it/vistoli/clifford.pdf
 |website=Scuola Normale Superiore
 |year=2007
}}</ref><ref name="ConradRootCalc" />

Closely related, though not itself an isomorphism between different classical-group families, is the exceptional [[triality]] automorphism of [[Spin(8)]].<ref name="Vistoli" /><ref name="ConradRootCalc" />

== Real forms ==

The same low-rank coincidences produce corresponding isomorphisms for noncompact real forms. In particular,
<math display="block">
\mathrm{Spin}^+(1,2) \cong \mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb R),\qquad
\mathrm{Spin}^+(1,3) \cong \mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb C),\qquad
\mathrm{Spin}^+(2,2) \cong \mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb R)\times\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb R),
</math>
and similarly
<math display="block">
\mathrm{Spin}^+(1,4) \cong \mathrm{Sp}(1,1),\qquad
\mathrm{Spin}^+(2,3) \cong \mathrm{Sp}(4,\mathbb R),
</math>
as well as
<math display="block">
\mathrm{Spin}^+(2,4) \cong \mathrm{SU}(2,2),\qquad
\mathrm{Spin}^+(3,3) \cong \mathrm{SL}(4,\mathbb R),\qquad
\mathrm{Spin}^+(1,5) \cong \mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb H)\cong \mathrm{SU}^*(4).
</math>
Here <math>\mathrm{Spin}^+</math> denotes the [[identity component]] of the corresponding spin group. Depending on convention, these relationships may also be presented as central [[isogeny|isogenies]] or as isomorphisms of the associated [[Lie algebra]]s.<ref name="Zemel">{{cite arXiv
 |last=Zemel
 |first=Shaul
 |title=An Algebraic Description of the Exceptional Isogenies to Orthogonal Groups
 |class=math.GR
 |eprint=1410.1397
 |year=2014
}}</ref><ref name="Bryant">{{cite book
 |last=Bryant
 |first=Robert L.
 |chapter=Pseudo-Riemannian metrics with parallel spinor fields and vanishing Ricci tensor
 |title=Global Analysis and Harmonic Analysis
 |series=Séminaires et Congrès
 |volume=4
 |publisher=Société Mathématique de France
 |location=Paris
 |year=2000
 |pages=53–94
 |arxiv=math/0004073
}}</ref>

== Explicit constructions ==

These exceptional isomorphisms can be constructed by exhibiting small linear representations that preserve a nondegenerate quadratic form. In each case one obtains a homomorphism to some <math>\mathrm{SO}(p,q)</math> with kernel <math>\{\pm I\}</math>, and the source group is thereby identified with the corresponding spin group. The various signatures arise by taking different real forms of the same complex construction.<ref name="GarrettSporadic">{{cite web
 |last=Garrett
 |first=Paul
 |title=Sporadic isogenies to orthogonal groups
 |url=https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~garrett/m/v/sporadic_isogenies.pdf
 |website=University of Minnesota
}}</ref><ref name="Zemel" /><ref name="Bryant" />

=== Dimension 3 ===

The 3-dimensional cases come from conjugation on [[traceless]] <math>2\times 2</math> matrices.<ref name="Zemel" /><ref name="Bryant" /> If
<math display="block">
V=\{x\in M_2(k):\operatorname{tr}(x)=0\},
</math>
with quadratic form
<math display="block">
q(x)=-\det(x)
</math>
(equivalently <math>q(x)=\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(x^2)</math>), then the action
<math display="block">
g\cdot x=gxg^{-1}
</math>
preserves <math>q</math>. Over <math>\mathbf C</math> this gives a homomorphism
<math display="block">
\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbf C)\to \mathrm{SO}(3,\mathbf C).
</math>
Choosing the compact or split real form yields
<math display="block">
\mathrm{SU}(2)\to \mathrm{SO}(3),\qquad
\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbf R)\to \mathrm{SO}(2,1).
</math>

A closely related construction gives the [[Lorentzian metric|Lorentzian]] case.<ref name="Zemel" /><ref name="Bryant" /> Let <math>V</math> be the real vector space of [[Hermitian matrix|Hermitian]] <math>2\times2</math> complex matrices, again equipped with the quadratic form <math>q(x)=-\det(x)</math>. Then <math>\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbf C)</math> acts by
<math display="block">
x\mapsto gxg^*,
</math>
preserving <math>q</math>. This is the usual action on [[Minkowski space]] and gives
<math display="block">
\mathrm{Spin}^+(1,3)\cong \mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbf C).
</math>

=== Dimension 4 ===

The 4-dimensional cases come from left and right multiplication on <math>M_2(k)</math>.<ref name="Zemel" /><ref name="Bryant" /> The quadratic form is again the determinant,
<math display="block">
q(x)=\det(x),
</math>
which is preserved by the action
<math display="block">
(g,h)\cdot x=gxh^{-1}.
</math>
Over <math>\mathbf C</math> this gives
<math display="block">
\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbf C)\times \mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbf C)\to \mathrm{SO}(4,\mathbf C),
</math>
while over <math>\mathbf R</math> it gives
<math display="block">
\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbf R)\times \mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbf R)\to \mathrm{SO}(2,2).
</math>
On the quaternionic real form one recovers the compact case
<math display="block">
\mathrm{SU}(2)\times \mathrm{SU}(2)\to \mathrm{SO}(4),
</math>
and hence
<math display="block">
\mathrm{Spin}(4)\cong \mathrm{Sp}(1)\times \mathrm{Sp}(1)\cong \mathrm{SU}(2)\times \mathrm{SU}(2).
</math>

=== Dimension 5 ===

The 5-dimensional cases are obtained from trace-free self-adjoint matrices.<ref name="Zemel" /><ref name="Bryant" /> For quaternionic Hermitian <math>2\times2</math> matrices, the reduced-trace quadratic form on the trace-free subspace is 5-dimensional and is preserved by
<math display="block">
x\mapsto gxg^*,
</math>
where the adjoint is taken with respect to the Hermitian form on <math>\mathbb H^2</math> of the appropriate signature. This yields homomorphisms
<math display="block">
\mathrm{Sp}(2)\to \mathrm{SO}(5),\qquad
\mathrm{Sp}(1,1)\to \mathrm{SO}(4,1),
</math>
and therefore the exceptional isomorphisms
<math display="block">
\mathrm{Spin}(5)\cong \mathrm{Sp}(2),\qquad
\mathrm{Spin}^+(1,4)\cong \mathrm{Sp}(1,1).
</math>

A split analogue uses the symplectic involution on <math>M_4(\mathbf R)</math>. The trace-free symplectically self-adjoint subspace is again 5-dimensional, and conjugation by <math>\mathrm{Sp}(4,\mathbf R)</math> preserves its quadratic form. This gives
<math display="block">
\mathrm{Spin}^+(2,3)\cong \mathrm{Sp}(4,\mathbf R).
</math>

=== Dimension 6 ===

The 6-dimensional cases come from the [[exterior power|exterior square]] of a 4-dimensional module. On <math>\Lambda^2(k^4)</math> there is a natural symmetric bilinear form defined by<ref name="Zemel" /><ref name="Bryant" />
<math display="block">
x\wedge y=\langle x,y\rangle\,\omega,
</math>
where <math>\omega\in \Lambda^4(k^4)\setminus\{0\}</math> is a fixed volume form. Since <math>\mathrm{SL}(4,k)</math> preserves <math>\omega</math>, it preserves this bilinear form. Over <math>\mathbf C</math> this gives
<math display="block">
\mathrm{SL}(4,\mathbf C)\to \mathrm{SO}(6,\mathbf C),
</math>
and over <math>\mathbf R</math> it gives
<math display="block">
\mathrm{SL}(4,\mathbf R)\to \mathrm{SO}(3,3).
</math>

Further real forms arise from additional structures on <math>\mathbf C^4</math>. If <math>\mathbf C^4</math> is equipped with a positive-definite Hermitian form, a Hermitian form of signature <math>(2,2)</math>, or a quaternionic structure, then the induced conjugate-linear involution on <math>\Lambda^2\mathbf C^4</math> has a real 6-dimensional fixed subspace on which the same bilinear form has signature <math>(6,0)</math>, <math>(4,2)</math>, or <math>(5,1)</math>. This yields
<math display="block">
\mathrm{Spin}(6)\cong \mathrm{SU}(4),\qquad
\mathrm{Spin}^+(2,4)\cong \mathrm{SU}(2,2),\qquad
\mathrm{Spin}^+(1,5)\cong \mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbf H)\cong \mathrm{SU}^*(4).</math>

In all of these constructions the kernel is <math>\{\pm I\}</math>, so the maps are the standard double covers of the corresponding special orthogonal groups.<ref name="Zemel" /><ref name="ConradRootCalc" /><ref name="KMRT" /> These constructions realize geometrically the low-dimensional root-system equalities
<math display="block">
A_1=B_1=C_1,\qquad
A_1\times A_1=D_2,\qquad
B_2=C_2,\qquad
A_3=D_3.
</math>

== General fields ==

The exceptional isomorphisms between classical groups extend beyond the split case and admit a uniform description over arbitrary fields using [[central simple algebra]]s with [[*-algebra|involution]].<ref name="KMRT" /><ref name="ConradOq" /> In this formulation, orthogonal, symplectic, and unitary groups arise from algebras equipped with involutions, and the low-rank coincidences <math>B_2=C_2</math> and <math>A_3=D_3</math> persist for all such forms.<ref name="KMRT" /><ref name="ConradOq" />

More precisely, the isomorphism <math>B_2=C_2</math> identifies symplectic groups attached to degree-4 algebras with symplectic involution with spin groups attached to 5-dimensional quadratic spaces, via constructions involving trace-zero symmetric elements and the Pfaffian norm.<ref name="KMRT" /><ref name="ConradOq" /> Similarly, the isomorphism <math>A_3=D_3</math> relates unitary groups of degree 4, defined using a quadratic [[étale algebra]] and a unitary involution, to spin groups in dimension 6, via [[Clifford algebra]]s and [[discriminant algebra]]s.<ref name="KMRT" /><ref name="ConradOq" /> In the split case these constructions reduce to the realization on <math>\Lambda^2 F^4</math>, but over general fields they describe all inner and outer forms of the corresponding groups.<ref name="KMRT" /><ref name="ConradOq" />

These phenomena are controlled by [[Galois cohomology]], which classifies forms of [[reductive algebraic group]]s.<ref name="SerreGC">{{cite book
 |last=Serre
 |first=Jean-Pierre
 |title=Galois Cohomology
 |publisher=Springer
 |location=Berlin
 |year=1997
}}</ref> The exceptional isomorphisms therefore identify not only the split groups but also their twisted forms over [[local fields|local]] and [[global field]]s.<ref name="KMRT" /><ref name="SerreGC" /> This has consequences in the theory of [[automorphic form]]s and the [[Langlands program]], where low-rank orthogonal and general spin groups are often studied via symplectic, linear, or unitary groups using [[Langlands functoriality|functorial transfer]] and [[theta correspondence]].<ref name="AsgariShahidi">{{cite journal |last1=Asgari |first1=Mahdi |last2=Shahidi |first2=Freydoon |title=Generic transfer for general spin groups |journal=Duke Mathematical Journal |volume=132 |issue=1 |year=2006 |pages=137–190 |doi=10.1215/S0012-7094-06-13214-3}}</ref><ref name="AsgariChoiy">{{cite journal
 |last1=Asgari
 |first1=Mahdi
 |last2=Choiy
 |first2=Kwangho
 |title=The local Langlands conjecture for p-adic GSpin4, GSpin6, and their inner forms
 |journal=Forum Mathematicum
 |volume=29
 |issue=6
 |year=2017
 |pages=1261–1290
 |doi=10.1515/forum-2016-0213
 |arxiv=1510.02553
 |mr=3719299
}}</ref>
===Overview===
Over a field <math>F</math> of characteristic different from 2, the low-rank exceptional isomorphisms of root systems <math>B_2=C_2</math> and <math>A_3=D_3</math> give rise to corresponding isomorphisms (or central isogenies) among classical algebraic groups.<ref name="KMRT" /><ref name="ConradOq" /> In the split case, these include
<math display="block">\operatorname{Spin}_5 \cong \operatorname{Sp}_4,\qquad \operatorname{SO}_5 \cong \operatorname{PGSp}_4,\qquad \operatorname{GSpin}_5 \cong \operatorname{GSp}_4,</math>
and
<math display="block">\operatorname{Spin}_6 \cong \operatorname{SL}_4,\qquad \operatorname{SO}_6 \cong \operatorname{PGL}_4.</math>
These identifications arise from explicit constructions: for <math>B_2=C_2</math>, from the action of <math>\operatorname{Sp}_4</math> on the 5-dimensional irreducible summand of <math>\Lambda^2 F^4</math>; and for <math>A_3=D_3</math>, from the action of <math>\operatorname{SL}_4</math> on <math>\Lambda^2 F^4</math>.<ref name="KMRT" /><ref name="ConradOq" />

The non-split forms can be described using [[central simple algebra]]s with involution.<ref name="KMRT" /><ref name="ConradOq" /> Let <math>A</math> be a simple algebra over <math>F</math> with center <math>Z(A)</math>. An involution <math>\sigma:A\to A</math> is said to be of the first kind if it acts trivially on <math>Z(A)</math>, and of the second kind otherwise. In the latter case, <math>Z(A)</math> is a quadratic étale extension <math>K/F</math> (that is, either <math>K=F\times F</math> or a [[separable field extension|separable]] quadratic field extension), and <math>\sigma</math> induces the nontrivial <math>F</math>-automorphism of <math>K</math>. Involutions of the first kind are further classified as orthogonal or symplectic, while those of the second kind are called unitary.<ref name="KMRT" />

For the exceptional isomorphism <math>A_3=D_3</math>, the non-split form may be described as follows. On the <math>A_3</math> side, one considers a central simple algebra <math>B</math> of degree 4 over a quadratic étale algebra <math>K/F</math>, equipped with a unitary involution <math>\tau</math>. On the <math>D_3</math> side, one considers a central simple algebra <math>A</math> of degree 6 over <math>F</math>, equipped with an orthogonal involution <math>\sigma</math>. There is a canonical correspondence between such pairs <math>(B,\tau)</math> and <math>(A,\sigma)</math>, under which one obtains isomorphisms of algebraic groups
<math display="block">\operatorname{SU}(B,\tau)\cong \operatorname{Spin}(A,\sigma),\qquad \operatorname{PGU}(B,\tau)\cong \operatorname{PGO}^+(A,\sigma).</math>
In the split case <math>K=F\times F</math> and <math>B\cong M_4(F)</math>, this reduces to the classical identifications <math>\operatorname{SL}_4\cong \operatorname{Spin}_6</math> and <math>\operatorname{PGL}_4\cong \operatorname{SO}_6</math>.<ref name="KMRT" /><ref name="ConradOq" />

For <math>B_2=C_2</math>, the non-split form relates symplectic and orthogonal groups. If <math>(A,\tau)</math> is a central simple algebra of degree 4 over <math>F</math> with symplectic involution, then there is a canonically associated 5-dimensional quadratic space <math>(V,q)</math>, and corresponding isomorphisms
<math display="block">\operatorname{Sp}(A,\tau)\cong \operatorname{Spin}(V,q),\qquad \operatorname{GSp}(A,\tau)\cong \operatorname{GSpin}(V,q),\qquad \operatorname{PGSp}(A,\tau)\cong \operatorname{SO}(V,q).</math>
Conversely, every 5-dimensional quadratic space arises in this way from the even Clifford algebra. In the split case this recovers the isomorphisms <math>\operatorname{Sp}_4\cong \operatorname{Spin}_5</math> and <math>\operatorname{PGSp}_4\cong \operatorname{SO}_5</math>.<ref name="KMRT" /><ref name="ConradOq" />

===Explicit constructions===
==== Split isomorphisms ====
In the split cases, the constructions are similar to the [[exceptional isomorphism]]s over the complex numbers.<ref name="KMRT" /><ref name="ConradOq" />

If <math>(W,\omega)</math> is a 4-dimensional symplectic space, then contraction with <math>\omega</math> defines a map <math>\Lambda^2W\to F</math>, and its kernel
<math display="block">\Lambda^2_0W=\ker(\Lambda^2W\to F)</math>
is a 5-dimensional subspace carrying a natural quadratic form preserved by <math>\operatorname{Sp}(W,\omega)</math>.<ref name="KMRT" /><ref name="ConradOq" />

For the <math>A_3=D_3</math> isomorphism in the split case, if <math>U</math> is a 4-dimensional vector space, then <math>\Lambda^2U</math> is 6-dimensional and carries a natural symmetric bilinear form, defined by identifying <math>\Lambda^4U</math> with <math>F</math>; this form is preserved by <math>\operatorname{SL}(U)</math>, giving the homomorphism <math>\operatorname{SL}_4\to \operatorname{SO}_6</math>.<ref name="KMRT" /><ref name="ConradOq" />

==== Non-split isomorphisms ====
To describe the non-split forms more explicitly, one uses standard constructions from the theory of central simple algebras with involution. Throughout this subsection, assume that the characteristic of <math>F</math> is not equal to 2.<ref name="KMRT" />

If <math>(A,\tau)</math> is a central simple algebra over <math>F</math> with symplectic involution, define
<math display="block">\operatorname{Sym}(A,\tau)=\{x\in A:\tau(x)=x\}.</math>
There is also a [[reduced trace]] map
<math display="block">\operatorname{Trd}_A:A\to F,</math>
which in the split case <math>A=M_n(F)</math> is the ordinary matrix trace. One defines the trace-zero subspace<ref name="KMRT" />
<math display="block">\operatorname{Sym}(A,\tau)^0=\{x\in \operatorname{Sym}(A,\tau):\operatorname{Trd}_A(x)=0\}.</math>

If <math>A</math> has degree 4, then <math>\operatorname{Sym}(A,\tau)^0</math> is a 5-dimensional vector space over <math>F</math>. The involution <math>\tau</math> determines a quadratic form on this space, called the [[Pfaffian]] norm, denoted <math>q_\tau</math>. In the split case <math>A=M_4(F)</math> with the standard symplectic involution, this quadratic form is the natural quadratic form on the 5-dimensional irreducible summand of <math>\Lambda^2 F^4</math>.<ref name="KMRT" /><ref name="ConradOq" />

More concretely, if <math>\operatorname{char}(F)\ne 2</math>, the reduced norm <math>\operatorname{Nrd}_A</math> satisfies
<math display="block">\operatorname{Nrd}_A(x)=q_\tau(x)^2 \qquad \text{for } x\in \operatorname{Sym}(A,\tau),</math>
and <math>q_\tau</math> is uniquely determined by this property. This quadratic form is nondegenerate on <math>\operatorname{Sym}(A,\tau)^0</math>.<ref name="KMRT" />

This construction yields the exceptional isomorphisms<ref name="KMRT" /><ref name="ConradOq" />
<math display="block">\operatorname{Sp}(A,\tau)\cong \operatorname{Spin}\bigl(\operatorname{Sym}(A,\tau)^0,q_\tau\bigr),</math>
<math display="block">\operatorname{GSp}(A,\tau)\cong \operatorname{GSpin}\bigl(\operatorname{Sym}(A,\tau)^0,q_\tau\bigr),</math>
<math display="block">\operatorname{PGSp}(A,\tau)\cong \operatorname{SO}\bigl(\operatorname{Sym}(A,\tau)^0,q_\tau\bigr).</math>

Conversely, if <math>(V,q)</math> is a 5-dimensional quadratic space, one forms its [[Clifford algebra]] <math>C(V,q)</math> and its even Clifford algebra <math>C_0(V,q)</math>. The algebra <math>C_0(V,q)</math> is a central simple algebra of degree 4 over <math>F</math>, equipped with a canonical symplectic involution <math>\tau</math>, and the above construction recovers <math>(V,q)</math> up to isomorphism.<ref name="KMRT" /><ref name="ConradOq" />

For the exceptional isomorphism <math>A_3=D_3</math>, one proceeds as follows. Let <math>K/F</math> be a quadratic étale algebra, and let <math>B</math> be a central simple algebra of degree 4 over <math>K</math> equipped with a unitary involution <math>\tau</math>. Thus <math>\tau</math> induces the nontrivial <math>F</math>-automorphism of <math>K</math> (Galois conjugation in the field case, or exchange of the two factors if <math>K=F\times F</math>).<ref name="KMRT" />

From <math>(B,\tau)</math> one constructs a central simple algebra <math>A</math> of degree 6 over <math>F</math>, equipped with an orthogonal involution <math>\sigma</math>, called the discriminant algebra of <math>(B,\tau)</math>. In the split case <math>B\cong M_4(F)\times M_4(F)^{\mathrm{op}}</math>, this corresponds to the action of <math>\operatorname{SL}_4</math> on <math>\Lambda^2 F^4</math>, which preserves a natural quadratic form and yields the isomorphism <math>\operatorname{SL}_4\cong \operatorname{Spin}_6</math>.<ref name="KMRT" /><ref name="ConradOq" />

Conversely, if <math>(A,\sigma)</math> is a central simple algebra of degree 6 over <math>F</math> with orthogonal involution, its Clifford algebra <math>C(A,\sigma)</math> has center a quadratic étale algebra <math>K/F</math>, and one obtains a degree-4 central simple algebra over <math>K</math> equipped with a canonical unitary involution. These constructions are mutually inverse up to isomorphism, and give<ref name="KMRT" /><ref name="ConradOq" />
<math display="block">\operatorname{SU}(B,\tau)\cong \operatorname{Spin}(A,\sigma),\qquad
\operatorname{PGU}(B,\tau)\cong \operatorname{PGO}^+(A,\sigma).</math>

=== Characteristic 2 ===

The preceding descriptions are simplest over fields of characteristic different from 2. In characteristic 2, the orthogonal side is more naturally expressed in terms of [[quadratic pair]]s rather than orthogonal involutions: if <math>(A,\sigma,f)</math> is a central simple algebra with quadratic pair, then <math>\sigma</math> is a symplectic involution, and the additional linear form <math>f</math> is needed to recover the corresponding quadratic form.<ref name="KMRT" /><ref name="ConradOq" />

(A quadratic pair on a central simple algebra <math>A</math> over a field <math>F</math> is a pair <math>(\sigma,f)</math>, where <math>\sigma</math> is an involution of the first kind on <math>A</math> and
<math display="block">
f:\operatorname{Sym}(A,\sigma)\to F
</math>
is a linear map satisfying
<math display="block">
f(x+\sigma(x))=\operatorname{Trd}_A(x)\qquad\text{for all }x\in A.
</math>
When <math>\operatorname{char}(F)\neq 2</math>, this notion is equivalent to that of an orthogonal involution, since <math>f</math> is then determined by <math>\sigma</math>. In characteristic <math>2</math>, however, an involution alone does not determine the corresponding quadratic data, and the extra linear form <math>f</math> is needed. Quadratic pairs are therefore the natural characteristic-2 analogue of orthogonal involutions.)<ref name="KMRT" />

For the exceptional isomorphism <math>B_2=C_2</math>, let <math>(A,\tau)</math> be a central simple algebra of degree 4 with symplectic involution. In characteristic 2, the relevant 5-dimensional quadratic space is built from the space
<math display="block">
\operatorname{Symd}(A,\tau)=\{x+\tau(x):x\in A\}
</math>
of symmetrized elements, rather than from <math>\operatorname{Sym}(A,\tau)</math>. More precisely, Knus–Merkurjev–Rost–Tignol identify the corresponding quadratic space with
<math display="block">
\bigl(\operatorname{Symd}(A,\tau)^0,s_\tau\bigr),
</math>
where <math>\operatorname{Symd}(A,\tau)^0</math> is the trace-zero subspace and <math>s_\tau</math> is the Pfaffian trace form. In this way the exceptional isomorphism persists in characteristic 2, but the orthogonal group is replaced by the group attached to this quadratic space, and the resulting map is best understood as an isogeny of algebraic groups rather than as a classical double cover with kernel <math>\{\pm I\}</math>.<ref name="KMRT" /><ref name="ConradOq" />

For the exceptional isomorphism <math>A_3=D_3</math>, the correct characteristic-2 object on the <math>D_3</math> side is a central simple algebra of degree 6 with quadratic pair <math>(A,\sigma,f)</math>. Its Clifford algebra is then a central simple algebra of degree 4 over a quadratic étale extension, equipped with a canonical unitary involution. Conversely, a degree-4 central simple algebra with unitary involution has an associated discriminant algebra of degree 6 with quadratic pair. Thus the equivalence between the <math>A_3</math> and <math>D_3</math> forms remains valid in characteristic 2, but it is expressed using quadratic pairs rather than orthogonal involutions.<ref name="KMRT" /><ref name="ConradOq" />

In the split case, the construction using the action of <math>\mathrm{SL}_4</math> on <math>\Lambda^2(F^4)</math> still gives the corresponding low-rank isogeny, but the invariant structure on the orthogonal side is again a quadratic pair. Likewise, the <math>B_2=C_2</math> construction may still be viewed through the 5-dimensional summand attached to a degree-4 symplectic algebra, provided it is formulated in terms of <math>\operatorname{Symd}(A,\tau)^0</math> and the quadratic form <math>s_\tau</math>.<ref name="KMRT" /><ref name="ConradOq" />

== Applications ==

The exceptional isomorphisms of classical groups have important applications in both mathematics and physics. In low dimensions they allow orthogonal and spin groups to be replaced by matrix groups of smaller degree, making many constructions more explicit. This is especially important in [[general relativity]], [[quantum mechanics]], [[twistor theory]], and the theory of [[automorphic form]]s. 

=== Spinor calculus in general relativity ===
The isomorphism
<math display="block">
\mathrm{Spin}^+(1,3)\cong \mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbf C)
</math>
is the basis of the [[two-spinor calculus]] used in four-dimensional Lorentzian geometry and [[general relativity]]. In this formalism, tensors on spacetime are rewritten in terms of spinor indices, and the [[Lorentz group]] acts through the defining 2-dimensional representation of <math>\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbf C)</math>. This makes it possible to express null vectors, [[Weyl curvature|Weyl]] and [[Ricci curvature]], and many field equations in a particularly compact form. The compact real form
<math display="block">
\mathrm{Spin}(3)\cong \mathrm{SU}(2)
</math>
likewise governs the spin degrees of freedom associated with spatial rotations. <ref name="PenroseRindler1">{{cite book
 |last1=Penrose
 |first1=Roger |author-link=Roger Penrose
 |last2=Rindler
 |first2=Wolfgang |author-link2=Wolfgang Rindler
 |title=Spinors and Space-Time. Vol. 1: Two-Spinor Calculus and Relativistic Fields
 |publisher=Cambridge University Press
 |location=Cambridge
 |year=1984
}}</ref>

=== Pauli and Dirac matrix formalisms ===
The same low-dimensional isomorphisms underlie the use of [[Pauli matrices]] and [[gamma matrices]] in quantum mechanics and relativistic quantum theory. The Pauli matrices realize the Lie algebra of <math>\mathrm{SU}(2)</math> and describe spin-1/2 systems under ordinary spatial rotations, while the double covering
<math display="block">
\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbf C)\to \mathrm{SO}^+(1,3)
</math>
allows Lorentz vectors to be represented by Hermitian <math>2\times2</math> matrices and Lorentz transformations to be expressed by
<math display="block">
X\mapsto AXA^*.
</math>
This is the standard bridge between two-component spinors, four-vectors, and the matrix formalism used in relativistic wave equations.<ref name="PenroseRindler1" /><ref>{{cite web
 |last=Hestenes
 |first=David
 |title=Applied Geometric Algebra
 |url=https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/res-8-001-applied-geometric-algebra-spring-2009/61e22b2382d47758078a4e5f8c239f20_aga-main_2009.02.02.pdf
 |website=MIT OpenCourseWare
}}</ref><ref>{{cite web
 |last=Haber
 |first=Howard E.
 |title=Exponentiating the Lie algebra of the Lorentz group
 |url=https://scipp.ucsc.edu/~haber/webpage/LTspinor.pdf
 |website=University of California, Santa Cruz
}}</ref>

=== Twistor theory and conformal geometry ===
Twistor theory uses the exceptional isomorphism
<math display="block">
\mathrm{Spin}^+(2,4)\cong \mathrm{SU}(2,2),
</math>
which identifies the spin group of the conformal group of four-dimensional Minkowski space with a unitary group of signature <math>(2,2)</math>. Twistor space is naturally a complex 4-dimensional vector space equipped with an <math>\mathrm{SU}(2,2)</math>-invariant Hermitian form, and the conformal geometry of spacetime is encoded in the incidence relation between spacetime points and projective lines in twistor space. In this way, the exceptional isomorphism is built into the basic symmetry group of twistor geometry.<ref name="PenroseRindler2">{{cite book
 |last1=Penrose
 |first1=Roger
 |last2=Rindler
 |first2=Wolfgang
 |title=Spinors and Space-Time. Vol. 2: Spinor and Twistor Methods in Space-Time Geometry
 |publisher=Cambridge University Press
 |location=Cambridge
 |year=1986
}}</ref><ref>{{cite arXiv
 |last=Adamo
 |first=Tim
 |title=Lectures on twistor theory
 |year=2017
 |arxiv=1712.02196
 |class=hep-th
}}</ref>

=== Automorphic forms and the Langlands program ===
Exceptional isomorphisms also play a role in the theory of automorphic representations by allowing low-rank orthogonal and spin groups to be studied through symplectic or linear groups. For example, the identification
<math display="block">
\mathrm{GSpin}_5 \cong \mathrm{GSp}_4
</math>
relates automorphic forms on a general spin group to the well-developed theory of Siegel modular forms of genus 2, while
<math display="block">
\mathrm{Spin}_6 \cong \mathrm{SL}_4
</math>
and related isogenies connect low-rank orthogonal groups with linear groups. These identifications are used in the formulation of [[Langlands functoriality]], local and global transfer, and instances of the [[local Langlands correspondence]].<ref name="AsgariShahidi" /><ref name="GanTakeda">{{cite journal
 |last1=Gan
 |first1=Wee Teck
 |last2=Takeda
 |first2=Shuichiro
 |title=The local Langlands conjecture for GSp(4)
 |journal=Annals of Mathematics
 |series=2
 |volume=173
 |issue=3
 |year=2011
 |pages=1841–1882
 |doi=10.4007/annals.2011.173.3.12
 |mr=2800725
}}</ref><ref name="AsgariChoiy" />

=== Conformal field theory and string theory ===
A related application occurs in conformal and superconformal field theory, where
<math display="block">
\mathrm{Spin}^+(2,4)\cong \mathrm{SU}(2,2)
</math>
identifies the spin group of the four-dimensional conformal group with the bosonic symmetry group appearing in many formulations of conformal field theory. In the best-known example, the symmetry supergroup of the <math>\mathrm{AdS}_5\times S^5</math> correspondence is <math>\mathrm{PSU}(2,2|4)</math>, whose bosonic part contains <math>\mathrm{SU}(2,2)</math> and <math>\mathrm{SU}(4)</math>; these are the exceptional low-rank real forms corresponding to <math>\mathrm{Spin}(2,4)</math> and <math>\mathrm{Spin}(6)</math>.<ref>{{cite journal
 |last=Maldacena
 |first=Juan
 |title=The large N limit of superconformal field theories and supergravity

 |volume=2
 |issue=2
 |year=1998
 |pages=231–252
 |doi=10.4310/ATMP.1998.v2.n2.a1
|bibcode=1998AdTMP...2..231M
 }}</ref><ref>{{cite arXiv

 |first=Arkady A.

}}</ref>
